headline: Shift Grid Costs to Large Users
short_summary: This bill aims to reduce residential electricity costs by requiring large energy users, such as data centers, to bear more of the financial burden for grid infrastructure upgrades and capacity.
supporters: Residential consumer advocates, environmental groups, Senator Mark Warner, Dominion Energy (supports amended bill).
news_headline: Virginia bill aims to cut power bills by shifting costs to data centers
news_summary: A Virginia bill is in motion to make data centers shoulder more energy costs, potentially saving residential customers over $65 annually. If passed, data center costs would increase to roughly 16%, while residential rates would drop from 3.5% to 3%.

headline: Data Center Water Use Reporting
short_summary: This bill mandates water users supplying data centers to report monthly or quarterly water consumption, including reclaimed water, to the State Water Control Board for transparency and environmental planning.
supporters: Environmental groups, water conservation advocates, local governments, Senator Kannan Srinivasan.
news_headline: New Virginia law requires data center water usage be made public
news_summary: A new Virginia law, effective January 1, 2027, mandates local water authorities to report data center water usage to the Department of Environmental Quality's website. This aims to provide transparency amid concerns about the industry's significant water consumption.

headline: Data Center Siting and Noise Limits
short_summary: This bill requires site assessments for new high energy use facilities, including data centers, to examine sound profiles on nearby residential units and schools, and allows localities to assess other environmental impacts.
supporters: Local communities, residential groups, environmental advocates, local governments.
news_headline: Virginia HB 153: Data Center Siting and Noise Limits Approved
news_summary: HB 153, approved by the Governor on April 13, 2026, requires site assessments for new high energy use facilities to examine sound profiles on residential units and schools. It also allows localities to assess impacts on water, agriculture, parks, historic sites, and forestland.
